title: Relative clauses 2: clauses with and without who/that/which
subtitle: the keys (that) you lost
summary: Keep who/that/which when it is the subject of the relative clause, and leave it out when it is the object.

lesson.heading: Subject: you must use who/that/which
lesson.text: In *The woman **who lives** next door to me is a doctor*, **who** = the woman, and the woman is the person who *lives* next door. Who is the **subject** of the relative clause, so you cannot leave it out.

examples.text: The woman **who lives** next door to me is a doctor.
Where are the keys **that were** on the table?
The people **who work** in the office are very friendly.

lesson.heading: Object: you can leave it out
lesson.text: In *The woman **who I wanted to see** was away*, **I** is the subject and **who** (= the woman) is the object of *see*. When who/that/which is the object, you can leave it out.

examples.text: The woman **I wanted to see** was away.
examples.note: or The woman who I wanted to see ...

examples.text: Did you find the keys **you lost**?
examples.note: or ... the keys that you lost?

examples.text: The dress **Lisa bought** doesn't fit her very well.

lesson.heading: Do not repeat the object
lesson.text: The relative clause already contains the object, so we do not add *it / them / him* at the end.

lesson.heading: Where the preposition goes
lesson.text: In relative clauses the preposition (**to / in / for / with** etc.) stays with the verb, at the end of the clause.

examples.text: Do you know the woman Tom is talking **to**?
examples.note: two sentences: Tom is talking to a woman. Do you know her?

examples.text: The bed I slept **in** wasn't comfortable.
Are these the books you were looking **for**?
The man I was sitting next **to** on the plane talked all the time.

lesson.note: Again, we do not repeat the object: the books you were looking for (not ~~looking for them~~).

left.label: noun + (that)
left.text: After everything, all the money, the best thing etc.
examples: I gave her all the money **(that) I had**.
I'll do the best **(that) I can**.

right.label: what = the thing(s) that
right.text: What starts the clause with no noun in front of it.
examples: I don't agree with **what you said**.
Tell me **what you want** and I'll try to get it for you.

lesson.text: Ask who does the verb in the relative clause. If the answer is the noun itself, keep who/that/which; if it is somebody else, you can drop it.

exercises.prompt: The woman ___ next door is a doctor.
exercises.explanation: Who is the subject of lives, so it cannot be left out.

exercises.statement: The dress Lisa bought doesn't fit her very well.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Lisa is the subject and the dress is the object, so that can be left out.

exercises.statement: The people work in the office are very friendly.
exercises.explanation: The people who work in the office are very friendly. Who is the subject here, so we must keep it.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order to ask about some lost books.
exercises.answer: Did you find the books you were looking for
exercises.explanation: The preposition for stays at the end of the relative clause.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the sentence you would say.

pairs.left: A friend is wearing a dress and you like it.
pairs.right: I like the dress you're wearing.

pairs.left: You wanted to visit a museum, but it was shut.
pairs.right: The museum I wanted to visit was shut.

pairs.left: Your friend had to do some work and you want to know if she has finished.
pairs.right: Have you finished the work you had to do?

pairs.left: You rented a car and it broke down after a few miles.
pairs.right: The car I rented broke down after a few miles.

pairs.left: You invited people to your party and some of them couldn't come.
pairs.right: Some of the people I invited to the party couldn't come.

exercises.prompt: A friend told you about a hotel. You ask: What's the name of the hotel ___?
exercises.explanation: The preposition about goes at the end, and that can be left out because it is the object.

exercises.prompt: You applied for a job but didn't get it. Unfortunately I didn't get the job ___.
exercises.explanation: The job is the object of applied for, so the relative pronoun can be dropped.

exercises.prompt: Gary is a good person to know. He's somebody ___.
exercises.explanation: Keep the preposition on at the end - and do not add him.

exercises.statement: What happened to the money was on the table?
exercises.explanation: What happened to the money that was on the table? Here that is the subject of was, so we cannot leave it out.

exercises.prompt: Why do you blame me for everything ___ wrong?
exercises.explanation: After everything we use that, not what.

exercises.prompt: I don't agree with ___ you said.
exercises.explanation: There is no noun before the clause, so we use what = the things that.

exercises.prompt: I don't trust him. I don't believe anything ___.
exercises.explanation: After anything we can leave the relative pronoun out - and we never add it at the end.
